title: Bhumia's promises
hookLine: tradition says a robber promised Nanak never to lie, harm the poor or betray a host, and the promises changed him

cards: A rich man keeps an open kitchen. Holy men passing through his district eat well at his table and leave praising his generosity. Nobody says aloud where the money comes from: robbery.
Bhumia, the sakhis call him, a landholder who raids by night and feeds saints by day. Then Nanak comes through, sits at the table, and doesn't eat. Bhumia wants to know why.

teach.b: In the sakhi, Nanak tells him plainly: food bought with stolen money isn't something he'll eat. Bhumia says he can't give up robbing; it's who he is. So Nanak, the story goes, asks for something smaller.
Three promises. Never tell a lie. Never harm the poor.
Never betray anyone whose salt you have eaten, whose food you've shared. Bhumia agrees. Those sound easy.
That night he sets out to rob the king's palace, dressed so finely the guards take him for a nobleman. One asks who he is, and he remembers promise one.

teach.h: A THIEF, HE SAYS. THE KING'S SALT.
teach.b: A thief, he says. The guard laughs and waves him in. Inside, he gathers treasure, and in the dark he tastes something from a dish.
Salt. The king's salt. Promise three.
He sets the treasure down and leaves with nothing. In the morning the palace finds things moved and nothing taken. The king's men find Bhumia, and asked straight out, he tells the truth.
Tellings differ on what the king did next, but they agree the robber was a changed man, and that he found Nanak again and gave up robbery for good.
Nanak didn't demand a whole new life at once, only three small promises.
They didn't change Bhumia's mind first. They changed what he could do, one night at a time, until there was no room left for the old life.

how: Sikhs retell the sakhi of Bhumia the robber as a story about honest earning and keeping one's word.

o: three small vows that turned a robber around
a ransom Bhumia promised the king's guards
the debts Bhumia's guests swore to repay him

games.q: inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: a thief, he tells the guard
never betray one whose salt you've eaten

s: in the sakhi, Nanak demands Bhumia give up robbery at once
he asks for three smaller promises instead.
Bhumia left the palace with nothing because he had tasted the king's salt
promise three: never betray one whose salt you have eaten.
every telling agrees on what the king did next
tellings differ, but agree the robber was changed.

games.q: you're Bhumia, inside the palace with the treasure gathered. in the dark you taste something from a dish, and it's salt. what do you do?
o: take the treasure; it was only salt.
set it down and leave with nothing.
games.why: he had promised never to betray one whose salt he'd eaten. he left with nothing, and the promises kept working.

practice: Choose one small promise, like Bhumia's: small enough to say yes to tonight, real enough to matter, like I won't lie about this one thing, or I'll keep the confidence a friend gave me. Word it plainly, and say it once, quietly.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath.

wordCard.voice: Bhumia's promises. Never lie, never harm the poor, never betray one whose salt you've eaten: the three small promises that, in the sakhi, turned a robber around.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a word given, a promise.

carryVoice: Your line: promises change us. That ends a week of sakhis: the learned man of Benares, Farid's successor, the king of the island, Mardana's last song, the boy who feared the fire, two villages, and Bhumia. Day seven hundred forty-two.
